selected.hook_line: Why does the strongest rush happen near the broken window, not across the whole cabin?
selected.viewer_expectation: If cabin pressure suddenly drops, air and loose objects should be pulled equally from every part of the cabin.
selected.visible_contradiction: A ribbon beside the opening snaps toward it, while another farther away moves much less.
selected.frame_zero: A sealed aircraft-window pressure rig has one open test port; the nearby ribbon is stretched hard toward it while the distant ribbon barely moves.
selected.character_action: He compares the two ribbons, pauses at the difference, then reaches for the storybook beside the rig.
selected.reaction: A focused glance turns into quiet surprise when the two ribbons do not behave the same way.
selected.activity: Comparing airflow close to and far from a sudden opening in a pressurized cabin model.
selected.location: A simple aircraft pressure-test room with a full-size cabin window rig.
selected.topic_link: Cabin air moves toward a new opening because pressure inside is higher than pressure outside.
selected.factual_anchor: At high altitude, cabin pressure is higher than outside pressure. If the pressure barrier breaks, air can rush outward until the pressure difference becomes smaller.
selected.payoff: A broken pressure window can cause rapid decompression and strong airflow near the opening, rather than equal pulling force everywhere.

entry_bridge.a_end: He places the storybook flat beside the pressure rig, one hand leaving the cover.
entry_bridge.b_start: Top-down, host-free view of the closed topic-styled book resting flat.
entry_bridge.reveal: The important force comes from the pressure difference between cabin air and the thin outside air.
entry_bridge.world_entry: A cabin cutaway shows air rushing outward through one open window while nearby loose objects move toward it.

novelty.tension_family: equal pull versus local strong flow
